newsitem.title: INDIA: India backtracks on scope of tax amnesty scheme.
newsitem.headline: India backtracks on scope of tax amnesty scheme.

text.p: India on Wednesday backtracked on the scope of a tax amnesty scheme launched earlier in the day and barred persons under investigation for violating foreign exchange laws from taking advantage of it.

Earlier on Wednesday, the authorities had said the amnesty scheme offered tax evaders, even those under investigation under the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act (FERA), the opportunity to come clean without penalty, raising some eyebrows.
The Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme (VDIS), which had been broadly outlined in the 1997/98 budget presented in February, would begin on July 1 and end on December 31.
The scheme aimed to draw tax evaders who operate in the shadows of the "parallel economy" into the tax net.
It already bars people who have been detained under FERA from taking advantage of the scheme.

"Where proceedings have been initiated against a person under FERA or a summons has been issued to him or an enquiry is pending against him or a prosecution has been launched against him, it is obvious that he cannot puport to 'disclose' any income, which is the subject matter of such proceedings," a Finance Ministry statement said.
"Hence, no unusual benefit will be conferred under the VDIS upon persons who are facing enquiries or proceedings or prosecution under FERA," the statement added, reversing the earlier announcement.
Private economists say at least four out of every 10 rupees earned in India are generated in the black economy and are never declared to authorities.
Ravi Kant, chairman of the Central Board of Direct Taxes, earlier told a news conference: "We want 100 percent integration of the parallel economy with the mainstream."
But he refused to put a figure on the size of the black economy. "We do not want to hazard a guess," he said.
The Finance Ministry has launched a media blitz to highlight the scheme and hired a public relations firm.
In the budget, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram slashed the tax rate for the highest personal income bracket to 30 percent from 40, and the corporate tax rate to 35 percent from 40.

"The government needs to get 300 to 400 billion rupees ($8.4 billion to $11 billion) to come in through this scheme or else it would serve no purpose," said V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce.
Officials cautioned that VDIS offered the last chance for tax evaders to come clean. "We do not really expect the need for these schemes in the future," Kant said.

Of the money raised through the scheme, 77.5 percent will go to the states and the balance will remain with the federal government. The money will be used to develop infrastructure, as well as health and education projects throughout the country. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
